title: Confined Space Entry Safety
summary: Manholes, crawl spaces, and tunnels can hold low oxygen, toxic or explosive gas, water, and other hazards, and would-be rescuers die too. This talk covers testing, monitoring, and never entering unprepared.
talking_points: Treat every confined space as hazardous. Ask your supervisor to walk through the written confined space program and emergency plan.
Get the training your employer is required to provide before you enter.
Test the air for oxygen level, flammable gases and vapors, and toxic contaminants before anyone goes in.
Check for water and electrical hazards, and inspect the structure so it will not collapse or drop material.
Never enter without an attendant monitoring you and a reliable way to communicate with someone outside.
Use the PPE your employer provides for the known hazards, such as a self-contained breathing apparatus. Leave right away if you see an unsafe condition.
site_hazards_to_check: Space not tested for oxygen, flammable gas, or toxic contaminants before entry
No attendant stationed outside and no communication method
No rescue plan or rescue equipment on site
Signs of structural weakness or loose material overhead inside the space
Standing water, energized equipment, or engine exhaust near the opening
discussion_questions: What could be in the air in this space, and who tests it before we enter?
Who is the attendant, and how do you signal them if something goes wrong?
If someone collapses inside, what is the rescue plan, and why should you not rush in?

flags: OSHA mapping verified accurate: 29 CFR 1926.1203 (permit-required confined spaces - general requirements) and 1926.1204 (permit-required confined space program), Subpart AA. Content - treat every confined space as hazardous, written program and training before entry, pre-entry atmospheric testing (oxygen, flammables, toxics), attendant plus reliable communication, rescue plan/equipment, employer-provided PPE incl. SCBA, evacuate on any warning sign - aligns with the standard.

Non-blocking enhancement: consider adding forced-air ventilation/purging as a listed control and continuous atmospheric monitoring during entry (not only pre-entry testing), and citing 29 CFR 1926.1211 (rescue) given the talk's emphasis on would-be rescuer fatalities.
